unit.title: Perform gas metal arc welding process to AWS specification (Pipe and plate)

summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to weld carbon steel pipe and plate with gas metal arc welding (GMAW, or MIG) to a welding procedure specification (WPS) under the AWS code the Centre uses. You will learn how procedures and welders are qualified, how to choose and control the transfer mode, gas and wire, and how to weld plate grooves on backing, open-root pipe joints and pipe-to-plate fillets in the fixed positions. You will also learn to find and prevent defects, test and record welds, do the job calculations, and plan and lead the work safely.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **gas metal arc welding (GMAW)** of pipe and plate to a code: groove welds on plate with steel or ceramic backing, open-root butt welds on pipe, and fillet welds joining pipe to plate, in the positions and with the transfer mode the WPS gives. In Jamaican workshops the process is usually called **MIG**; with argon/CO2 gases on steel it is strictly MAG (metal active gas).

GMAW is fast and clean, but its short-circuit mode can leave **lack of fusion** that cannot be seen on the surface and may not show on a radiograph. That is why the codes treat it with care, and why a Level 3 welder must understand the procedure, record real values, and test the welds, not just make them look good.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other providers, and welders who lead MIG work on structural steel, handrails, posts, frames and pipework.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Work to the code and WPS
Know when a procedure must be qualified by test, read the WPS and PQR, and keep inside the ranges.
Check qualifications
Check that a welder's WPQ covers the process, transfer mode, positions, direction, thickness and diameter of the job.
Set up the equipment
Set up the power source, wire feeder, gun, gas and work return for plate and for pipe on rolls, and check real values with meters.
Choose and control the transfer
Choose short-circuit, spray or pulsed transfer, the gas and the wire, and set wire speed, voltage and inductance to get it.
Weld plate
Weld single-V grooves on steel or ceramic backing in the 1G–4G positions.
Weld pipe
Weld open-root pipe butts (1G, 2G, 5G, 6G) uphill or downhill as the WPS says, and pipe-to-plate fillets (2F, 2FR, 4F, 5F).
Find and prevent defects
Recognise lack of fusion, porosity, burn-through, cracking and arc blow, and cure them.
Inspect, test and record
Inspect visually; know bend, macro, MT, UT and RT tests; record PQR-style data and weld logs.
Calculate, plan and lead
Work out weld metal, wire, gas, arc time and output; plan the job, brief the team and keep it safe.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on specifications and WPSs, qualification, positions, backing, pipe roots, inspection, arc blow, equipment, technique, wire, gas, defects, testing, calculations, safety, finishing, distortion and leading the team.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms or figures (for example metal-cored, mixed gas, 2F, 4F, PH, short-circuit, argon, MT, burnback, work lead, single bevel, contact tip, or a worked number) and essays in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: single-V groove coupons in 10 mm plate in the 3G and 4G positions on ceramic backing, with bend tests and draft WPQs; and an open-root pipe butt in the 5G position and a pipe-to-plate fillet in 5F, with visual inspection, macro etches and a PQR-style record.

blocks.note: Questions at this level ask why a procedure is written the way it is, and what went wrong when a weld fails. Learn the reason behind each rule: most of them are there to stop lack of fusion.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Under the AWS structural code, some procedures are **prequalified**: if every detail (joint design, process, filler, position, settings) stays inside the code's limits, the WPS can be used without a test. Others must be **qualified by test**: a test weld is made, the real values are recorded and the weld is tested, and the results go on a **PQR**. Short-circuit GMAW (GMAW-S) is **not prequalified** under that code, because it puts in little heat and can leave lack of fusion on the side walls, so a short-circuit procedure must always be qualified by test. Check what the code or procedure the Centre uses says for each job.

head: Document
What it holds
rows: WPS

Process and transfer mode; base metal and thickness range; pipe diameter range; joint design and backing; wire class and size; gas and flow; polarity; wire feed speed, current and voltage ranges; travel speed; stick-out; positions and progression (uphill or downhill); preheat and interpass; technique and cleaning
PQR
The actual values used on the test weld (measured, not guessed) and the results of the visual and mechanical tests
WPQ
A welder's test record and the range of work it covers
Weld log and weld map
Which welder made each weld, with which WPS, wire batch and gas, and the inspection results

ul: **Wire feed speed** sets the current on a constant-voltage set, so it is recorded with the current.
**Voltage** is read with a checked meter at the arc (between the gun or feeder and the work). If the set's own display reads differently, record the true arc value and report the set for checking.
**Travel speed** is found by timing a measured length of weld.
**Gas** type and flow, measured with a flowmeter.
**Joint dimensions** (bevel, root face, gap) are measured before welding; **temperatures** with crayons or a thermometer.
The welder and the witness sign the record.

blocks.p: A change in an essential variable needs a new or revised WPS, qualified by test where the code says. For GMAW these include: the **transfer mode** (for example short-circuit to spray, or the reverse), the **shielding gas**, the **wire classification**, the base metal group and thickness range, the joint design and backing, a big change in heat input, the **position** and the **progression** (uphill or downhill). A new cylinder of the same gas, a different qualified welder, or a new contact tip are not procedure changes.

ul: **Process and transfer mode**: a welder who passed a test with spray or pulsed transfer is not qualified for short-circuit work, and the reverse.
**Positions**, from the test position, and the **progression**: uphill and downhill are qualified separately.
**Thickness**: a thicker test plate (for example 25 mm) covers a wider thickness range than a 10 mm one.
**Pipe and plate**: a pipe test generally covers plate, but a plate test does not cover small-diameter pipe.
**Continuity**: a welder who has not used the process for a set period (often six months) must be re-tested.

blocks.note: When a welder brings a WPQ from another company, check that it is signed and current, that it covers this job's process, transfer mode, positions, direction and thicknesses, and that their continuity is recorded, before they weld on your job.
blocks.label: Remember

How it is set
ISO letters
rows: 1G plate / 1G pipe
Flat plate; or pipe rolled with the axis horizontal, welded on top
PA
2G
Weld axis horizontal: plate upright, or pipe with its axis vertical
PC
3G (plate)
Vertical, welded up or down

Overhead
PE

Axis horizontal and fixed; welded round, up or down

Axis fixed at 45°
H-L045 (up), J-L045 (down)

head: Pipe-to-plate fillet
How it is set
rows: 2F
Pipe axis vertical, standing on the plate; the weld runs round level, made from above
2FR
Pipe axis horizontal and the pipe rotated, so the weld is always made in the horizontal-fillet position at the top
4F
Pipe axis vertical, with the plate above; the weld is made from below, overhead
5F
Pipe axis horizontal and fixed; the weld runs round through overhead, vertical and flat

sections.title: Safety for GMAW on pipe and plate

head: Hazard
Controls
rows: Arc radiation: GMAW gives very strong ultraviolet, more than stick welding at the same current
Helmet with the right shade (often about 11–13; follow the chart); all skin covered; screens; warn others
Fume and ozone
Extraction at the arc; head out of the plume; respirator where extraction is not enough
Wire inching: the wire can shoot out of the gun and pierce skin or an eye
Never point the gun at anyone, or at yourself, while inching or loading wire
Turning rolls: nip points between pipe and wheels; pipe rolling off
Guards at the nip; set the wheels for the pipe size; only the operator controls the rolls; keep hands and clothing clear
Heavy pipe and plate
Lifting gear, safety boots and gloves; chock loose pipe so it cannot roll; clamp pipe stands firmly
Gas cylinders; argon in low places
Chain cylinders upright; close valves after use; ventilate pits and trenches
Electric shock
Dry gloves; sound cables and gun; work lead on the job close to the weld
Hot coupons and spatter
Mark hot work; use tongs; cap, closed collar and done-up sleeves for overhead work
Fire
Clear combustibles; extinguisher at hand; fire watch after the work
Etching chemicals
Goggles, gloves and an apron; ventilation; read the SDS; used under supervision

blocks.h: Shutting down at the end of the shift

flow: Release the trigger and let the post-flow finish; hang the gun up, never on the work
Close the gas cylinder valve, then press the trigger (or the purge button) to bleed the gas out of the line
Wind the regulator out, switch the set off and coil the cables
Cover the wire spool or return it to the dry store
Mark hot coupons, clean the bay and report any faults

blocks.note: Most Jamaican shops are open-sided. A breeze that cools you also blows the gas shield away from a MIG arc and causes porosity. Use screens on the windward side, and keep spools covered, because humid air rusts bare wire quickly.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: GMAW uses a **constant-voltage** power source on **DC electrode positive (DCEP)** for steel. The voltage is set on the power source; the **wire feed speed** sets the current. Many modern sets are **synergic**: you choose the wire and gas, set one value, and the set matches the other.

head: Part or setting
Its job
Points to know
rows: Voltage
Sets the arc length
Too low: the wire stubs into the plate and the bead is tall and ropey. Too high: a long arc, spatter, undercut, and in short-circuit a change towards globular transfer
Wire feed speed
Sets the current and the amount of metal laid
Set with the voltage as a matched pair
Inductance
In short-circuit, controls how fast the current rises each time the wire touches the pool
More inductance: a softer, wetter, hotter arc with less spatter. Less: a crisper, colder arc with more spatter
Burnback
Lets the wire burn back a little after the trigger is released
Too short: the wire is left stuck in the crater. Too long: the wire melts back onto the contact tip
Crater fill
Lowers the wire speed and voltage at the end of a weld
Fills the crater and prevents crater cracks
Pre-flow and post-flow
Gas before the arc starts and after it stops
Protect the start and the crater
2T / 4T trigger
2T: weld while the trigger is held. 4T: press to start, press again to stop
4T eases long welds round a pipe
Pulse programs
Switch the current between a high peak and a low background many times a second
Spray-like transfer at a lower average heat, usable in all positions

ul: Use **V-groove** drive rolls for solid steel wire, at just enough pressure to feed it without slipping.
Fit a liner to suit the wire size, and keep the gun cable as straight as you can.
The **contact tip** must match the wire size; replace it when its hole is worn or full of spatter.
For short-circuit work the tip usually sits level with the nozzle or slightly out; for spray it is usually set back inside the nozzle.
Keep the nozzle clean of spatter: a blocked nozzle spoils the gas cover.

blocks.p: Keep a short, steady stick-out: often about 10–15 mm for short-circuit transfer and about 15–25 mm for spray. A longer stick-out heats the wire more, so on a constant-voltage set the current falls and penetration drops; that matters most on an open pipe root, where penetration must stay even all round.

ul: Fix the work lead on clean metal on the job, close to the weld.

When pipe turns on rolls, connect the work lead with a **rotating clamp** on the pipe. Never let the current pass through the bearings of the rolls, and never hold the pipe by hand to complete the circuit.
Read the voltage at the arc with a checked meter, and the current with a checked clamp meter.
Time a run-out of wire to check the wire feed speed.
Check the gas flow with a flowmeter, and for leaks at the connections.
If the set's own displays disagree with the checked meters, record the checked values and report the set.

head: Mode
How it works
Positions and uses
Watch for
rows: Short-circuit (GMAW-S)
Low current and voltage; the wire touches the pool many times a second and each touch transfers a drop
All positions; thin metal, open roots, gaps
Low heat: lack of fusion on side walls and on thick plate. Must be qualified by test under the AWS structural code
Globular
Large, irregular drops fall across the arc; common with 100% CO2 at higher currents
Flat and horizontal
Spatter; rarely chosen on purpose
Spray
Above the transition current, with an argon-rich gas (about 80% argon or more), a fine stream of droplets crosses the arc without short circuits
Flat, and horizontal fillets only: the pool is large and fluid
High heat and deposit rate; deep penetration; needs thick enough metal
Pulsed spray
The current pulses between a spray-level peak and a low background
All positions, with lower average heat; pipe and plate
Needs a pulse-capable set, the right gas and a program covered by the WPS

blocks.p: Some sets offer **controlled short-circuit** waveforms that shape the current through each short circuit. They are used for open pipe roots because they give steadier penetration with less spatter; they still need a qualified WPS.

head: Gas
Use
rows: Argon with about 15–25% CO2
The usual all-round gas for short-circuit on carbon steel; can give pulsed transfer on suitable sets
Argon with about 5–10% CO2, or 1–5% oxygen
Spray and pulsed transfer on carbon steel
Short-circuit only; deep penetration, more spatter; no true spray
Pure argon
Not for carbon steel: the arc is unstable and the weld wets and fuses poorly. Used for aluminium

ul: Typical flow is about 12–20 L/min, as the WPS says. More is not better: high flow becomes turbulent and pulls air in.
The gas is set by the WPS. A welder may not swap to a different gas because it "spatters less": gas is an essential variable.

head: Class
Features
Use
rows: ER70S-6
Solid; high manganese and silicon deoxidisers
Most common; copes with light mill scale and rust
ER70S-3
Solid; fewer deoxidisers
Clean plate; general work
ER70S-2
Solid; extra deoxidisers (aluminium, titanium, zirconium)
Roots, and plate that is not perfectly clean
E70C-6M (metal-cored)
A steel tube filled mostly with metal powder. C = composite (metal-cored); M = classified with a mixed argon/CO2 gas
Higher deposit rate than solid wire of the same size, a wider and more forgiving arc and good side-wall fusion; very little slag; costs more

ul: Common solid wire sizes: 0.8, 0.9, 1.0 and 1.2 mm. Small pipe roots in short-circuit often use 0.9 mm (or 0.8–1.0 mm).
Solid wire is usually copper-coated. It leaves no slag cover, only small brown glassy **silicon islands** that must be brushed or ground off between passes.
Keep spools dry and covered. Rusty wire causes porosity and poor feeding.
Prepare and fit up exactly as the WPS shows: groove angle, root face, root gap and backing. A **single-V** has both edges bevelled; a **single bevel** has one edge bevelled and the other left square.
The groove must be no narrower than the WPS angle: in a narrow groove the gun cannot reach to fuse the side walls.
Clean to bright metal, including the backing: mill scale, rust, paint, oil and moisture cause porosity.

head: Backing
How it works
Points to know
rows: Steel backing strip
A strip tacked under the root; the root fuses into it and it stays on the job
Must sit tight against both plates; a gap traps slag and leaves lack of fusion
Ceramic backing
Ceramic tiles on aluminium adhesive tape, pressed under the joint
Supports and shapes the root, then is removed, so no backing is left on the job. Centre the tiles under the gap, press the tape down firmly, and leave no gaps between tiles

ul: **Gun angle**: a push (forehand) angle of about 5–15° gives a flatter, wider bead, good gas cover and a clear view of the joint; a drag angle gives a narrower bead with deeper penetration.
Keep the arc on the **leading edge of the pool**. If the pool runs ahead of the arc, it lies on cold plate without fusing: the classic cause of lack of fusion in short-circuit GMAW.
**Starting**: strike a little ahead of the start point and move back over it, or start on a run-on tab, so the cold start is melted in.
**Stopping**: use crater fill, or pause and fill the crater, and keep the gun in place during post-flow.
Clean every pass: brush off silicon islands and grind humps.

head: Position
Technique
rows: 1G flat
Short-circuit or spray as the WPS says; stringers or a slight weave on fill and cap
2G horizontal
Stack stringer beads from the bottom up; tilt the gun slightly upward on the lower beads to stop the metal sagging
3G vertical
Uphill with short-circuit or pulsed transfer: a slight weave, pausing at the sides; downhill only on thin material where the WPS allows it
4G overhead
Short-circuit or pulsed; small pool, narrow stringers or small weaves, steady travel; full protection from falling spatter

blocks.note: Spray transfer makes a large, fluid pool. It is used only in the flat position and for horizontal fillets. Vertical and overhead welds are made with short-circuit or pulsed transfer.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Check the bevels, root face and gap against the WPS; clean the bevels and 25 mm inside and out to bright metal
Line the pipes up with an even gap; check the inside step between the bores with a hi-lo gauge
Tack at equal spacing (for example three or four tacks); grind each tack thin and feather its ends
Check the gap again after tacking; fix the coupon or spool in the stand at the right position and do not move it during the test

blocks.note: A step (hi-lo) between the two bores leaves one edge of the root higher than the other. The arc cannot fuse the high edge properly, leaving incomplete penetration or a notch inside. Fix it at fit-up, not with the welding.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Keep a **short, steady stick-out**, so the current, and therefore the penetration, stays even all round the joint.
Keep the arc at the front of the pool and watch both edges fuse; a small keyhole shows that the root is going through.
**Burn-through** on thin wall, with the fit-up right: travel a little faster, or bring the settings down within the WPS.
After the root, lightly grind the top of it to remove humps and the cold edges along its sides, so the next pass fuses fully. Then lay the hot pass.

head: Progression
How it is done
Why it is used
rows: Downhill (PJ)
Start just past the top (12 o'clock) and weld down each side to just past the bottom, overlapping the starts and stops. Travel fast enough that the pool never runs ahead of the arc
Fast; good for short-circuit roots on thinner wall
Uphill (PH)
Start just past the bottom and weld up each side to just past the top. A slight weave, pausing at the sides
Slower, hotter and better fusion into the side walls: often used for fill and cap passes, even when the root is downhill

blocks.p: Weld in the progression the WPS gives. Uphill and downhill are different procedures and different welder qualifications: a welder who prefers the other direction is stopped, and either welds to the WPS or a new procedure is qualified.

ul: **1G rolled**: the pipe turns on rolls under the gun and the pool stays in the flat position near the top. Set the roll speed so the pipe surface passes at the WPS travel speed: revolutions per minute = travel speed ÷ circumference.
**2G**: stack stringers from the bottom up; tilt the gun slightly upward on the lower beads so the metal does not sag.
**6G**: weld as for 5G, with the stringers on the cap laid from the lower side of the joint upward.

blocks.p: On DC, magnetism in the pipe can push the arc to one side, so it wanders, spatters and fails to fuse. It is worst at the ends of joints and on pipe that has been magnetised, for example by magnetic lifting or magnetic particle testing.

ul: Move the work clamp, or use two clamps, so the current flows a different way.
Weld towards a heavy tack, or away from the clamp; use run-on and run-off tabs on plate.
Wrap a few turns of the work cable round the pipe to cancel the field, or have the pipe demagnetised.
Keep a short arc.
Set the pipe square to the plate (check with a square), and tack in three or four places.
Aim the arc a little more at the **thicker** member, usually the plate, so both are fused and the legs come out even.
In **5F**, the position changes from overhead to vertical to flat as you go round: change the gun angle as you go, and weld each half as the WPS directs.
Welding a post on rolls (**2FR**) keeps every part of the weld in the easy horizontal-fillet position.
To finish a weld that runs right round, carry the end over the start by about 10–15 mm so it fuses into it, then fill the crater.
Test by eye and with a fillet gauge, then cut and etch macros at several places round the joint, because the fusion can change as the position changes.

blocks.p: A base plate welded all round in one long run can dish as the weld shrinks. Clamp the plate down (or bolt two plates back to back), weld in balanced parts on opposite sides, and use a jig so every post is set square and at the same height.

head: Defect
Main causes
Prevention
rows: Lack of fusion (cold lap)
Short-circuit on thick plate or a narrow groove
Pool running ahead of the arc (travel too slow, especially downhill)
Too little heat; long stick-out; poor gun angle
Right transfer mode for the thickness
Arc on the front of the pool; correct travel speed
Settings and stick-out to the WPS; correct groove angle
Porosity
Wind or draughts; flow too low or too high; blocked nozzle; leaks
Rust, mill scale, paint, oil or moisture; rusty wire
Screens; correct flow; clean nozzle
Clean to bright metal; dry, clean wire
Burn-through and excess penetration
Too much heat for the wall; gap too wide; travel too slow
Correct fit-up; faster travel or lower settings within the WPS
Incomplete root penetration
Gap too small; root face too thick; too little heat; hi-lo
Fit up to the WPS; correct line-up
Centre-line cracking
A bead much deeper than it is wide, as with spray in a narrow, deep groove
Keep beads wider than they are deep; correct groove angle and settings
Undercut
Voltage or travel speed too high; wrong angle
Correct settings; pause at the toes
Spatter
Voltage too low or too high; too little inductance; wrong gas; dirty plate
Correct settings and gas; clean plate; anti-spatter on the nozzle
Arc strikes
Striking outside the joint
Strike only in the joint or on a tab

blocks.note: Lack of fusion in short-circuit GMAW is often thin and flat, lying along the side wall. A radiograph can miss it, because there is almost no gap for the X-rays to show. Bend tests, macro etches and ultrasonic testing are much better at finding it.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Before**: joint preparation, gap, hi-lo, backing, cleanliness, settings recorded.
**During**: real values, progression, interpass, cleaning, the root inside (mirror) before the hot pass.
**After**: size and profile, undercut, overlap, porosity, cracks, spatter, arc strikes; the root inside the pipe for penetration and concavity.
Remove spatter before final inspection and painting: it can hide faults and spoils the coating.
How much undercut, reinforcement or porosity is allowed is set by **the code and the job specification**, not by the welder.

head: Test
What it finds
Points to know
rows: Visual (VT)
Surface faults, size, profile
Always first; a coupon that fails visual has failed
Bend tests (face, root, side)
Lack of fusion, porosity, cracks opened up
A strip that opens along the side wall shows lack of side-wall fusion
Macro etch
Fusion boundaries, penetration, leg size, profile
Several sections round a pipe joint
Magnetic particle (MT)
Cracks at and just below the surface of steel
Uses a magnet and fine iron powder; can leave the pipe magnetised
Ultrasonic (UT)
Internal faults, especially flat ones such as lack of fusion
Often added to radiography where lack of fusion is a worry
Radiography (RT)
Porosity, slag, lack of penetration
Can miss thin, flat lack of fusion

flow: Mark the coupon with the welder's identity before welding, and the top position on a pipe coupon
Check the coupon visually; only a coupon that passes is cut
Cut the strips from the places the code shows; remove the backing
Grind the cap and root flush and round the long edges slightly
Bend round the former in the guided bend jig, with the guards on
Judge the bent face against the code's limits, and record the result on the WPQ or PQR

head: What you need
How
Worked example
rows: Weld metal volume
Groove cross-section area × length
Weld metal mass
Volume (cm³) × 7.85 g/cm³
Wire needed
Weld metal ÷ deposition efficiency (solid wire often about 90–95%)
Gas used
Flow × arc time
15 L/min × 18 min = 270 L per joint
Total weld length on a pipe
Number of passes × length of one pass (π × diameter)
4 passes on 168.3 mm pipe: 4 × 528.8 ≈ 2 115 mm
Welder's time per joint
Arc time ÷ operating factor
12 min of arc at a 40% operating factor: 12 ÷ 0.40 = 30 min
Joints in a shift
Shift time ÷ (welding time + set-up time per joint), rounded down
8 h = 480 min; 40 + 8 = 48 min a joint: 480 ÷ 48 = 10 joints
Roll speed for 1G
Travel speed ÷ circumference
300 mm/min on 114.3 mm pipe: 300 ÷ 359 ≈ 0.84 rev/min

blocks.note: Keep units consistent: mm² × mm gives mm³, and 1 000 mm³ = 1 cm³. Write every step down and work the sum twice.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Study the drawing: pipe and plate sizes, weld sizes and symbols, positions, finish and tests
Check there is a WPS for each joint and position, and that each welder's WPQ and continuity cover it
Order and check pipe, plate, wire and gas against the drawing and the WPS
Make jigs so parts are set square and to the same height every time; plan for as many welds as possible in easy positions (rolled or on a positioner)
Plan the sequence to control distortion, and set the hold points
Brief the team; inspect the first item fully (by eye, with gauges and a square) before the rest are made
Keep the weld log; remove spatter; complete the records and hand over

ul: Check settings and progression on every station. A welder working outside the WPS, even with good-looking welds, is stopped and the welds already made are checked.
Never change the WPS by hand on the job: changes go through the proper approval, with a new PQR where needed.
Make sure every member knows the hazards: wire inching, turning rolls, overhead spatter, gas cylinders.
Record and report faults and near misses, and review the job with the team at the end.

**PQR-style record**: joint measurements, wire class, size and batch, gas and flow, transfer mode, wire speed, volts, amps, travel speed for each pass, position and progression, temperatures, and the test results, signed by the welder and witness.
**Weld log**: each weld's number, welder, date, WPS, wire batch, inspection and test results.
**Inspection reports** for visual, macro, bend, MT, UT or RT.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain prequalified and qualified procedures, and why short-circuit GMAW must be qualified by test under the AWS structural code.
I can record PQR values correctly, measuring volts at the arc and timing travel speed.
I can name the essential variables for GMAW, including transfer mode, gas and progression.
I can check a welder's WPQ against a job, including one from another company.
I can name the plate, pipe and pipe-to-plate positions, with their ISO letters.
I can control the hazards of GMAW, turning rolls, wire inching and gas, and shut a set down safely.
I can set voltage, wire speed, inductance, burnback, crater fill and stick-out, and check real values.
I can choose short-circuit, spray or pulsed transfer, and the gas and wire, for a job.
I can prepare and weld single-V plate grooves on steel or ceramic backing in 1G–4G.
I can weld an open-root pipe joint downhill or uphill as the WPS says, and prepare the root for the next pass.
I can weld pipe-to-plate fillets in 2F, 2FR, 4F and 5F with even legs.
I can control arc blow and distortion.
I can name the common GMAW defects, with their causes and cures, and explain why lack of fusion is hard to find.
I can prepare bend strips and macros, and read the results.
I can work out weld metal, wire, gas, arc time, output and roll speed.
I can plan and lead a GMAW job and keep the records.

terms: The arc being pushed to one side by magnetism, mainly on DC
A setting that lets the wire burn back after the trigger is released, so it does not stick in the crater
Ceramic tiles on tape that support and shape a root and are then removed
The copper part the wire passes through and picks up the current
A setting that lowers wire speed and voltage at the end of a weld
A change that needs a new or revised, qualified procedure
Gas metal arc welding with short-circuit transfer
The step between two pipe bores at a joint, checked with a hi-lo gauge
A setting that controls how fast the current rises in short-circuit transfer
Weld metal lying against the parent metal or a previous pass without melting into it
A tube filled mainly with metal powder, used with gas
Arc time as a percentage of the welder's total time on the job
Procedure qualification record: the measured values and test results that prove a WPS
A procedure the code allows without a test, within the code's limits
The direction of welding on vertical or fixed pipe work: uphill or downhill
Transfer in which the current pulses between a spray-level peak and a low background
A work-lead clamp that lets a pipe turn on rolls while carrying the current
Small glassy deposits left on a GMAW bead, removed between passes
A groove with one edge bevelled and the other left square
Fine droplets crossing the arc above the transition current, with argon-rich gas
The length of wire between the contact tip and the arc
A set that matches wire speed and voltage automatically from one setting
The current above which spray transfer starts
Powered wheels that turn a pipe under the gun for 1G welding
The cable that carries the welding current from the work back to the set
Welder performance qualification: a welder's test record and what it covers

c1.title: Floodlight posts for a sports complex in Anchovy
c1.text: A shop near Anchovy, St James, is making 16 floodlight posts for a sports complex: steel pipe of 114.3 mm outside diameter with a 6 mm wall, each welded to a 16 mm base plate with an 8 mm fillet all round, using GMAW. To keep the welding in an easy position, Sheldon, the team leader, has the posts laid with their axis horizontal on turning rolls, with the base plate clamped on, so the weld is made at the top as the post turns.

c2.title: Qualifying a procedure in Stony Hill
c2.text: A fabricator in Stony Hill, St Andrew, has won a job for steel stair stringers that calls for short-circuit GMAW to the AWS structural code. Natalie is recording the procedure test. A 180 mm length of the fill pass takes 40 seconds, and the checked meters at the arc read 19 V and 150 A. The owner asks whether, once the procedure is qualified, the crew can switch to spray transfer on the thicker plates "to speed things up".

c3.title: 5G pipe coupons at the Centre in Maggotty
c3.text: At a training centre in Maggotty, St Elizabeth, trainees are welding open-root 5G coupons in 114.3 mm carbon steel pipe with a 6 mm wall, using 0.9 mm ER70S-6 wire, argon with 25% CO2, a downhill short-circuit root and uphill fill and cap passes. Inside one coupon, the root has a thin unfused line at about 4–5 o'clock. At another station the wire keeps stubbing into the joint and pushing the gun back, and the bead stands tall and narrow. One trainee has left his tacks full height, with square ends.

c4.title: Irrigation spools on rolls in Bluefields
c4.text: A shop near Bluefields, Westmoreland, is welding irrigation pipe spools from carbon steel pipe of 219.1 mm outside diameter, turned on powered rolls under the gun. The WPS gives a travel speed of 350 mm/min. The pipe has light mill scale and some surface rust in places. At the end of each run, the welder finds the wire stuck in the frozen crater.

c5.title: Plate coupons on ceramic backing in Albert Town
c5.text: At a training centre in Albert Town, Trelawny, trainees weld single-V coupons in 10 mm plate in the 3G and 4G positions on ceramic backing, to a WPS that calls for pulsed or short-circuit transfer. One trainee has stuck the ceramic tiles on with gaps of about 3 mm between them, and the tape is lifting at one end. Another trainee's overhead fill passes sag and drip.

questions.q: What AWS position is Sheldon's set-up, with the post on the rolls and the weld made at the top as it turns?
o: 5F
2F
2FR
1G
questions.why: With the pipe axis horizontal and the pipe rotated so the weld is always made in the horizontal-fillet position, the position is 2FR. 5F is the same layout with the pipe fixed, and 2F has the pipe standing upright.

questions.q: How should Sheldon make sure all 16 posts end up square to their base plates?
o: Weld each one, then bend it square with a jack if needed
Use a jig, and check each post square before tacking
Tack each post by eye, as the rolls will square it up
Check only the last post, once all of them are welded
questions.why: A jig sets every post in the same place, and a square check before tacking catches errors while they can still be put right. Inspecting the first post fully before the rest are made stops one mistake being copied 16 times.

questions.q: How should the welder finish the fillet where it meets its own start, after one full turn?
o: Stop just short of the start and leave a small gap
Stop right on the start, then grind the join flush
Carry on round the joint a second full time to be sure
Run over the start by 10–15 mm, then fill the crater
questions.why: Carrying the end over the start melts in the cold start so the weld is continuous and fused, and filling the crater prevents a crater crack. A gap, or stopping short, leaves an unwelded spot.

questions.q: What is the travel speed of the fill pass?
o: About 450 mm/min
About 270 mm/min
About 220 mm/min
About 4.5 mm/min
questions.why: Travel speed = length ÷ time = 180 mm ÷ 40 s = 4.5 mm/s, × 60 = 270 mm/min. 4.5 is the figure per second, not per minute.

questions.q: Natalie works out the heat input of the pass from these readings. What is it, and what does it tell her?
o: About 6.3 kJ/mm: very high, so the steel will be weakened
About 0.06 kJ/mm: too low to melt the wire at all
About 0.63 kJ/mm: low, which is why fusion must be proved
About 1.27 kJ/mm: typical of spray transfer on thick plate
questions.why: Heat input = 19 × 150 × 60 ÷ (270 × 1 000) = 171 000 ÷ 270 000 ≈ 0.63 kJ/mm. This low figure is typical of short-circuit transfer, and is why its fusion must be proved by test.

questions.q: How should Natalie answer the owner's question about spray transfer?
o: Yes, as the welders are already qualified for GMAW
Yes, as long as the gas stays the same as on the PQR
No: a new transfer mode needs its own qualified procedure
No: spray transfer cannot be used on steel stair stringers
questions.why: Transfer mode is an essential variable: spray needs its own WPS (prequalified or qualified, as the code allows), the right gas, and welders qualified for spray. It also suits only flat and horizontal welds.

questions.q: Why does the code make the fabricator qualify a short-circuit procedure by test, instead of using it as prequalified?
o: Its low heat can leave hidden lack of fusion
Short-circuit welds always contain porosity
Short-circuit transfer needs a special gas mix
The welds are too small to inspect by eye
questions.why: Short-circuit transfer puts in little heat, so weld metal can lie on the side wall without fusing, and the fault may not show on the surface. Testing (bends, macros) proves that the procedure fuses properly.

questions.q: Where should the downhill root be started?
o: Just past the top, then down each side
At the bottom, welding up each side to the top
At 3 o'clock, welding all the way round in one go
Wherever the trainee is most comfortable starting
questions.why: A downhill (PJ) root starts just past 12 o'clock and runs down each side to just past 6 o'clock, overlapping the starts and stops so they fuse.

questions.q: What most likely caused the thin unfused line inside the root at 4–5 o'clock?
o: The gas mix had too much argon in it
The wire was 0.9 mm instead of 1.2 mm
The root gap was a little wider than usual
Travel was too slow, so the pool ran ahead
questions.why: On a downhill root the pool tends to run ahead of the arc if travel is too slow, and it then lies on cold metal without fusing. Keep the arc on the front of the pool and travel fast enough to stay ahead of it.

questions.q: What should be changed at the station where the wire stubs and the bead stands tall and narrow?
o: Raise the voltage to match the wire speed
Turn the gas flow up to about 30 L/min or more
Lengthen the stick-out to about 30 mm or more
Change to a larger contact tip size
questions.why: Stubbing and a tall, ropey bead mean the voltage is too low for the wire speed (or the wire speed too high for the voltage). Bring them into balance within the WPS ranges.

questions.q: One trainee leaves his tacks full height with square ends. What is the likely result where the root runs over them?
o: Lack of fusion or a hump at each tack
A stronger root, as the tacks add metal
Porosity right round the whole root
Burn-through just before every tack
questions.why: A short-circuit arc cannot melt into a thick, square-ended tack, so the root rides over it, leaving unfused edges and a hump. Grind tacks thin and feather their ends so the root fuses through them.

questions.q: About how fast must the rolls turn the pipe to give the WPS travel speed?
o: About 2.0 rev/min
About 1.6 rev/min
About 5.0 rev/min
About 0.5 rev/min
questions.why: Circumference = 3.142 × 219.1 ≈ 688 mm. Rev/min = 350 ÷ 688 ≈ 0.51. Dividing the other way round gives 2.0, and leaving out π gives 1.6.

questions.q: Which wire suits this pipe best, if the WPS allows the choice?
o: ER70S-3, which has fewer deoxidisers in it
ER70S-6, with high manganese and silicon
ER4043, an aluminium-silicon filler wire
ER308L, a low-carbon stainless steel wire
questions.why: ER70S-6 has the most manganese and silicon of the common steel wires, which deal with oxygen from light mill scale and rust. The surface should still be cleaned as well as possible.

questions.q: Which setting should be adjusted to stop the wire sticking in the crater?
o: Make the burnback time a little longer
Make the pre-flow time a little longer
Turn the gas flow right up
Turn the inductance down to minimum
questions.why: Burnback lets the wire keep burning for a moment after the trigger is released. Too short, and the wire is left in the pool as it freezes; too long, and it melts back onto the contact tip.

questions.q: What is likely to happen with the gapped tiles and lifting tape?
o: Nothing, as the ceramic only needs to cover the ends
The root will be stronger, since it can cool faster
Metal runs into the gaps and the root is uneven
The tape will burn off and give off toxic fume
questions.why: Ceramic backing must be centred under the gap, pressed tight, with no gaps between tiles. At gaps and loose tape the root sags, burns through or forms an uneven, porous lump that has to be ground out.

questions.q: The overhead fill passes sag and drip. Which change helps most?
o: A wider weave with a longer pause in the middle
Smaller stringer beads with steady travel
More voltage, to keep the pool fluid longer
Switch to spray transfer for a hotter arc
questions.why: Overhead, gravity pulls a large pool down. Smaller beads at the lower part of the WPS range, with steady travel, let each bead freeze before it can sag.

questions.q: Why does the WPS call for pulsed or short-circuit transfer for these coupons, and not spray?
o: Spray needs 100% CO2 gas, which is not allowed
Spray will not fuse into ceramic backing at all
Spray uses too little wire for 10 mm plate
Spray's large, fluid pool cannot be held up
questions.why: Spray transfer makes a big, hot, fluid pool, so it is used flat and for horizontal fillets only. Pulsed and short-circuit transfer give a smaller, controllable pool for vertical and overhead work.

questions.q: In short-circuit GMAW, the arc is harsh and crackly with heavy spatter, though the volts and wire speed are within the WPS. Which adjustment, if the WPS allows, softens it?
o: Less inductance
More inductance
A longer burnback
A shorter pre-flow
questions.why: Inductance slows the rise of current at each short circuit. More inductance gives a softer, wetter arc with less spatter; less gives a crisper, colder arc with more spatter.

questions.q: Compared with a drag angle, what does a push angle of about 10° usually give in short-circuit GMAW?
o: A narrower bead with much deeper penetration
More spatter and a rougher, higher bead
A flatter bead and a clear view of the joint
No need for shielding gas at the weld
questions.why: Pushing aims the arc ahead onto the joint, giving a flatter, wider bead, good gas cover and a clear view of where the weld is going. Dragging gives a narrower bead and deeper penetration.

questions.q: On an open-root pipe joint, the inside of one pipe sits 3 mm higher than the other. Why does this matter?
o: The root cannot fuse fully on the high edge
The pipe will be too heavy to lift afterwards
The shielding gas will escape through the step
The welder's qualification no longer applies
questions.why: A step between the bores (hi-lo) leaves one edge out of reach of the arc, giving incomplete penetration or a notch inside. Correct the line-up at fit-up, within the WPS or code limit.
